POLI 401.d: A research seminar in state politics and policy with an emphasis on state institutions.
POLI 401.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 591.d: Individualized study on a specific topic in the field of Methodology for Ph.D. students. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 591.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 526.d: A seminar on partisan polarization in the United States from both behavioral and institutional perspectives.
POLI 526.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 335.d: Study of the foundation of government involvement in public policy and the institutional process guiding executive, legislative, and bureaucratic officials. Includes theories of collective action and their application in the political world.
POLI 335.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 563.d: This course examines the extensive scholarship on coalition politics in parliamentary democracies. Topics include coalition formation, the allocation of government ministries, coalition termination, coalition policymaking, and the interaction between coalition governance, party competition, and mass voting behavior.
POLI 563.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 377.d: This course explores the range of theories and empirical research methodologies from comparative political science, political-economy, and Asian studies commonly applied to understanding Chinese politics: political participation, political organizations, collective action and popular protest, political culture, and political institutional change. This course will be a seminar requiring weekly presentations, extensive readings at the graduate level in social science, and an original research paper. There is no prerequisite for this course, but participants are assumed to already possess extensive knowledge of Chinese history, culture, and society. Cross-list: ASIA 377. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 377 if student has credit for ASIA 489/POLI 489.
POLI 377.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 360.d: A survey of government and politics in Western European democracies, with primary emphasis on Great Britain, France, and Germany.
POLI 360.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 479.d: This course examines the international dimensions of authoritarian politics, exploring how authoritarianism increasingly operates beyond national borders. It introduces core features of authoritarian rule and analyzes how regimes and their opponents engage with international institutions, foreign governments, and transnational actors in contemporary world politics.
POLI 479.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 677.d: Topics and credit hours vary each semester. Contact department for current semester's topic(s). Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 677.type: Internship/Practicum, Laboratory, Lecture, Seminar, Independent Study
POLI 677.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate or Visiting Graduate level students.

POLI 527.d: Theories of institutional analysis and design.
POLI 527.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 573.d: How does gender affect the onset, conclusion and experience of violent conflict? The class introduces students to major concepts and debates in this field. Students will learn to view social science questions through a gendered lens. This course focuses heavily on the research process, culminating in an original research proposal. Graduate/Undergraduate Equivalency: POLI 379.
POLI 573.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 307.d: This course provides credit for a student who is required to receive course credit for an internship related to political science. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 307.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 318.d: Analysis of presidential powers and behavior in the context of legal, electoral, personal, and other forces that shape and limit the actions of the President.
POLI 318.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 577.d: Graduate research seminar on the influence of domestic politics on international relations. The course will explore when, why, and how the political structures and conditions within countries affect foreign policy and international relations.
POLI 577.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 539.d: Broad survey of the theoretical and methodological approaches used in political psychology. Topics include political information processing, knowledge, attitudes, political trust, emotions, and personality.
POLI 539.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 503.d: Applications of least squares and general linear mode. Cross-list: STAT 503.
POLI 503.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 463.d: Seminar on the politics global supply chains (GSCs). Will study their imperial origins and legacies; their effects on the distribution of wealth and the trajectory of democratic rule. Will explore the weaponization of GSCs by governments and activists (e.g. hackers, insurgents, saboteurs).
POLI 463.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 373.d: Exploration of the theoretical basis of, and empirical evidence for, a number of explanations for interstate war. Includes contemporary theories dealing with dispute escalation, arms races, deterrence, crisis management, and low-intensity conflict.
POLI 373.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 459.d: Latin American countries have elected surprisingly large numbers of women to presidencies, cabinets, and legislatures in recent years. This seminar explores how this happened in a region long known for its culture of machismo and weak democracy and what the consequences of gender diversity are for politics.
POLI 459.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 466.d: Seminar on the determinants of party systems, the structure and functions of parties, and theories of voting behavior in Western democracies.
POLI 466.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 533.d: This course examines mass political behavior and the analytical frameworks used to understand it. Topics will include public opinion, vote choice, turnout, campaign contributions, and participation in social movements.
POLI 533.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 429.d: This course is an introduction to the biological underpinnings of political behavior. The influence of genes and evolution are covered, as well as the relevance of neural structures, brain organization, and neuro-chemistry for both universal political traits and individual variation in political orientations. NOTE: This seminar is in the theory and methods field. It is not an American politics seminar.
POLI 429.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 375.d: Study of the development and role of international organizations in world politics. Topics include the history and evolution of international organizations, the effects of international law on behavior, and the extent to which international cooperation has been effective at resolving global problems.
POLI 375.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 480.d: What do Americans know about politics and how does it matter for their political behavior? This course explores how information, uncertainty and misinformation influence political decision-making. It also considers how the public acquires factual beliefs and reviews efforts to correct political misperceptions and reduce knowledge deficits.
POLI 480.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 481.d: Understanding War and Peace: Why do countries resort to the use of military force, and how can such conflicts be resolved? This course will Introduce students to current research on the causes and consequences of international conflict. In addition to reading and discussing current scholarship, students will have the opportunity to engage in their own research.
POLI 481.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 418.d: The course examines the modern presidency since World War II with a focus on the extent to which the Trump presidency has influenced the office and been influenced by it. It specifically studies the ways in which a single president can change the office and the government. The examination considers the expansion of presidential power especially during war and its relation to the Constitution. It assesses the public presidency through television, the internet and social media. It investigates the organization of the White House and the nature of presidential decision-making. The central question is how much of a difference do individual presidents make to the office they hold.
POLI 418.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 376.d: This course explores patterns of and explanations for human rights violations over time, as well as international and domestic solutions to protect human rights.
POLI 376.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 567.d: In this course we will explore the nature and sources of cross-national differences in mass political behavior. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 567 if student has credit for POLI 358.
POLI 567.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 538.d: This course will explore policy and political change primarily, but not exclusively, in the United States. Using a political economy approach, we will explore different models of change and identify the actors, institutions, and conditions that facilitate stability in change in state, local and national policymaking.
POLI 538.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 531.d: Examines similarities and differences in the organization of state politics. Major issues include state legislative organization, state elite behavior, and policy implementation.
POLI 531.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 597.d: Individualized study on a specific topic in the field of Comparative Politics for Ph.D. students. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 597.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 454.d: The salience of identity in the study of politics is indisputable. In this course, we will explore key questions surrounding identity politics in the non-Western world. We examine how identities shape political behavior, the influence of external factors in shaping identity, and the ways politicians mobilize identities for their own advantage, among other topics. Graduate/Undergraduate Equivalency: POLI 521. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 454 if student has credit for POLI 521.
POLI 454.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 334.d: Examination of the American political party system both historically and contemporarily, with important emphasis on the nomination, campaign, and election functions of political parties. Party organization in government will also be explored.
POLI 334.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 379.d: How does gender shape violent conflict, and how does war transform gender relations? Drawing on feminist international relations and women’s and gender studies, this course examines how gendered norms and institutions influence war, peacebuilding, violence, and representation across diverse social and cultural contexts. Graduate/Undergraduate Equivalency: POLI 573.
POLI 379.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 366.d: This course introduces students to the complex issues of democracy and development in South Asia. It will shed light over the important political science topics in a comparative perspective. Topics that will be covered include regimes, identity (caste, religion, gender) and conflict, migration, and diaspora and immigration in the US.
POLI 366.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 595.d: Individualized study on a specific topic in the field of International Relations for Ph.D. students. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 595.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 450.d: The course examines the electoral process in Latin America. Students will follow, discuss, and analyze campaigns and elections in a selected group of countries while developing an expertise in the general functioning of the respective countries' political systems.
POLI 450.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 521.d: The salience of identity in the study of politics is indisputable. In this course, we explore key questions surrounding identity politics in the non-Western world. We examine how identities shape political behavior, the influence of external factors in shaping identity, and the ways politicians mobilize identities for their own advantage, among other topics. Graduate/Undergraduate Equivalency: POLI 454. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 521 if student has credit for POLI 454.
POLI 521.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 507.d: An initiation to machine learning tailored for social science research. We will acquaint participants with modern machine learning methods and their applications in the R programming language. We will then demonstrate various applications of machine learning techniques to answer research questions in the social sciences, such as the application of machine learning to causal inference.
POLI 507.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 380.d: Examines basic concepts in political behavior including political socialization, models of voting behavior, public opinion, and political participation.
POLI 380.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 363.d: This course introduces students to the study of leadership, with a focus on leadership in the political arena. Using a social science framework, we will examine the role of individuals as leaders of governmental and political bodies in shaping the culture, performance, and outcomes of those bodies.
POLI 363.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 800.d: Students enrolled in this course are engaged in Ph.D. level research. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 800.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 477.d: Topics and credit hours may vary each semester. Contact department for current semester's topic(s). Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 477.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 571.d: Seminar on causes, consequences and dynamics of civil wars. Will analyze why they break out, how sustained, how ended, thinking conceptually, theoretically, empirically about conflict dynamics and processes. Explores transnational dynamics, terrorism, roles of groups, organizations, insurgency-counterinsurgency dynamics and how these affect the evolution of civil conflicts. More work will be required of the Graduate level. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 571 if student has credit for POLI 469.
POLI 571.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 502.d: This course aims at providing students with a working knowledge of statistics in political science. It involves the study of descriptive and inferential statistics, as well as hands-on experience with computer statistical packages.
POLI 502.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 599.d: This course prepares graduate students to design and teach classes at the college level. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 599.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 359.d: This course introduces students to constitutional systems around the world with a focus on constitutional design. The course coves the basics of constitutional theory, drafting, and amendment, political institutions, and constitutional rights and liberties, often using constitutional case law to highlight the critical questions surrounding contemporary constitutional theory and design.
POLI 359.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 465.d: Seminar examining the politics of coalition formation, coalition governance, and coalition breakup in the European multi-party democracies in which coalition governments are the norm.
POLI 465.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 357.d: This course will examine the theory of democracy and the functioning of democratic institutions around the world. Themes covered in the course will include: What is democracy? How does democracy arise? Can institutions influence the survival and consolidation of democracy?
POLI 357.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 544.d: This course will teach graduate students how to design and conduct original empirical research on US, state, or world legislatures. Students will conduct original quantitative research and produce a publishable research paper. Instructor Permission Required.
POLI 544.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 541.d: Graduate seminar on theories and evidence of international cooperation. Discussion of the difficulties in establishing cooperation under anarchy and the conditions under which international cooperation is most likely to occur.
POLI 541.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 532.d: Provides the student with the basic concepts and theories necessary to understand the functions and organization of legislatures/parliaments/assemblies in democratic societies. This course takes a broad-based perspective, including research that focuses on national parliaments and U. S. state legislatures.
POLI 532.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 536.d: This course examines the causes and consequences of women’s underrepresentation in politics in countries around the world. It considers common theoretical frameworks for the study of women’s representation and the empirical bases of what we know about gender and political representation.
POLI 536.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 490.d: Study of the development of modern political theory and its relevance to contemporary problems. NOTE: This seminar is in the theory and methods field. It is not an American politics seminar.
POLI 490.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 534.d: Graduate research seminar in the subfields of interest groups and political behavior.
POLI 534.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 339.d: A survey of central topics in gender and politics, including issues such as women's and men's representation in government, women as voters and candidates in political elections, gender and political participation in political parties and social movements, and gender and policy representation.
POLI 339.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 370.d: The objective of this course is to understand the causes and consequences of corruption in politics and engage critically with cutting-edge research on corruption in the social sciences.
POLI 370.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 474.d: This course has two goals: First to introduce students to the current theoretical debates in the field of international organizations and to assess the value and limitations of these theories; second, to understand the working of important world organizations, including (but not limited to) the UN, the WTO, and IMF. The course assumes some basic knowledge of IR theory and previous debates about the origin and impact of international organizations on world politics. It is designed for students at an advanced stage in the study of political science and International Relations.
POLI 474.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 329.d: Applies an interdisciplinary approach to the study of health policy. Objectives are to provide students with a broad introduction to the healthcare system, identify stresses on the current system, and explore possible public policy decisions that may transform the healthcare system.
POLI 329.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 374.d: Introduction to the uses of game theory in the study of international relations.
POLI 374.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 593.d: Individualized study on a specific topic in the field of American Politics for Ph.D. students. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 593.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 467.d: An interdisciplinary course that will equip students with the analytical tools for understanding the dynamics driving the politics of migration and refugees globally. Students will examine why and how states try to control their borders, the factors that shape the making of migration policy, and different types of migration, with a particular focus on refugees.
POLI 467.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 511.d: Study of advanced topics in research design and measurement theory.
POLI 511.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 570.d: Seminar in international conflict. Emphasis on formal theories and quantitative analysis of the causes of war.
POLI 570.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 435.d: This course explores the possible ways money may affect American politics and public policy at the national, state, and local levels of government. In addition to discussing the strategies used in allocating money in campaigns, we will examine the impact of money on elections and on the legislative process.
POLI 435.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 330.d: Examination of the political and social position of minority groups (African Americans, Asian Americans, Native Americans, Latinos, and women) in the U.S. This course explores the political power and behavior of these groups. The key concepts include racism, discrimination, resources, political power, culture, leadership, class, and inequality.
POLI 330.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 212.d: This course introduces students to major topics in the subfield of Comparative Politics, including emergence and survival of democracy, authoritarian government, democratic institutions, and mass and elite political behavior in countries around the world. This course helps students navigate upper division courses in Comparative Politics and explore the political world.
POLI 212.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 367.d: This course explores the individual and societal forces that shape political attitudes and action. Students will learn where political choice comes from, with a cross-national perspective.
POLI 367.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 391.d: This course examines the decade-long war between Russia and Ukraine by understanding topics including the history of Russo-Ukrainian relations/identities; causes and consequences of relevant social movements (Orange Revolution, Euromaidan); escalation from the War in Donbas to the present; domestic/international responses to the war, and analyses of current events.
POLI 391.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 238.d: Topics and credit hours vary each semester. Contact department for current semester's topic(s). Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 238.type: Independent Study, Internship/Practicum, Laboratory, Lecture/Laboratory, Seminar, Lecture
POLI 238.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 414.d: A seminar examining the extent, causes, and consequences of partisan polarization in American politics. We will assess the degree of division among voters and political leaders and then evaluate whether and how American political and social institutions can function effectively in the era of polarization.
POLI 414.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 455.d: This seminar explores political behavior in democracies around the world. This includes studies of public opinion and political participation among mass publics, as well as political behavior of elite actors such as parties and politicians.
POLI 455.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 445.d: Thinking about law school? This seminar explores social scientific literature in judicial process and behavior and examines selected controversies in the study of judicial processes. Learning is based on active participation in seminars covering assigned readings and a research project on a related topic selected by the student.
POLI 445.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 568.d: Examines the design of political institutions in democracies, and their effect on elections, governance, and representation. Explores topics such as the presidential-parliamentary debate, electoral laws and party systems, political parties, electoral institutions and the election of women and minorities, institutional engineering, and U.S. experiences with alternative electoral systems.
POLI 568.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 469.d: Seminar on causes, consequences and dynamics of civil wars. Will analyze why they break out, how sustained, how ended, thinking conceptually, theoretically, empirically about conflict dynamics and processes. Explores transnational dynamics, terrorism, roles of groups, organizations, insurgency-counterinsurgency dynamics and how these affect the evolution of civil conflicts. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 469 if student has credit for POLI 571.
POLI 469.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 326.d: This course explores the appropriate relationships between the religious beliefs of the participants in a democracy and the laws and regulations adopted, particularly in the context of the dual commitments to democratic processes and separation of church and state. A broad introduction to the American Constitutional law of religious freedom is provided.
POLI 326.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 457.d: This course starts with definitions and theories/preconditions of democracy and then looks at specific cases of democratic transition throughout the world, democratic consolidation, reaction, and the prospects for the future.
POLI 457.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 478.d: This is a research seminar for advanced undergraduate students to read and discuss international relations theories in the context of US-China relations. Students are expected to read cutting edge IR research, follow current events, think critically of the applicability of the existing IR theories on the issues surrounding the bilateral relationship.
POLI 478.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 406.d: This is the second course in the Political Science Honors Program. Students will conduct independent research and write a thesis paper by the end of the semester. Students must complete both POLI 405 and 406 to get Honors in Political Science. Instructor Permission Required.
POLI 406.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 341.d: Introduces legal frameworks of analysis and sources of law pertaining to issues of racial equality and discrimination. Questions include: How has law been used to perpetuate inequality? How has law made it more difficult to achieve reforms to advance equality? How have law and legal institutions helped advance racial equality and justice?

POLI 434.d: This course will examine the market-like relationship among metropolitan area governments. It will address questions of urban/suburban relationships as well as policy topics such as education and local service provision.
POLI 434.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 592.d: Individualized study on a specific topic in the field of Methodology for Ph.D. students. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 592.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 110.d: This course provides credit for students who have successfully completed approved examinations, such as Advanced Placement exams. This credit counts toward the total credit hours required for graduation.
POLI 110.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 224.d: This experiential learning course teaches students how to run for elected office. Working in teams and with advice from election experts, campaign advisors, and former and current candidates and elected officials, students develop a campaign plan to win a specific local or state elected office.
POLI 224.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 325.d: Examination of race in U.S. politics. Includes a discussion of the construction of black identity, historical and contemporary black political leaders and thinkers, and the influence of race in political attitudes and behaviors.
POLI 325.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 470.d: Topic varies from year to year. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 470.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 392.d: A course on Jerusalem's past and present, its religious meanings in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, and its role in the modern conflict in the Middle East. Instructor Permission Required. Instructor Permission Required.
POLI 392.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 321.d: This course explores how the Supreme Court has interpreted and applied the nation's foundational document – the United States Constitution. In doing so, we will examine the powers of the federal and state governments, the executive’s emergency powers, and the Supreme Court’s authority to nullify the acts of other branches.
POLI 321.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 572.d: Study of foreign policy, its sources, and the process of policy formulation.
POLI 572.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 420.d: This multidisciplinary course will consider how elections are conducted to enhance participation, to accurately measure the will of the electorate, and to be sufficiently rigorous to convince all parties that the results are legitimate. This course will consider the design and evaluation of election technologies, ranging from voter registration through the polling booth and vote tabulation. This course will consider three questions: how do individual voters interact with the voting technology, how are voting technologies engineered to be accurate and secure, and how do the social aspects of voting fulfill democratic goals for elections? A central requirement for this course will be group research projects, many operating in our community, built around the November election. Cross-list: COMP 435, PSYC 420.
POLI 420.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 311.d: The objective of this course to develop an understanding of how race, ethnicity, historical context, and racism inform and interact with American public policy.
POLI 311.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 353.d: This course examines the functioning of the political system in the three principal East Asian democracies: Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. Particular focus is paid to each country's democratic institutions, electoral politics, and political party system. Cross-list: ASIA 353.
POLI 353.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 596.d: Individualized study on a specific topic in the field of International Relations for Ph.D. students. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 596.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 416.d: The major objectives of this course are to introduce students to the skills and resources needed to design and conduct a survey. The principle substantive focus of the course will be public opinion surveys on topics of politics, public policy and individual political behavior.
POLI 416.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 501.d: This course is a continuation of POLI 500. Students will plan and execute an original research project and write a paper reporting the results.
POLI 501.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 437.d: Examines educational politics and policy from micro and macro perspectives. We will focus on school governance, structure, and finance at the federal, state, and local levels and examine the design, implementation and effects of various school reform initiatives in U.S., and to a more limited extent in other countries.
POLI 437.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 369.d: This course introduces students to key concepts, themes, and approaches in the study of protests, civil resistance, and government response around the world. It surveys key recent findings on when protests happen as well as when and how they succeed.
POLI 369.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 542.d: Examines the role of subnational political institutions in the development and implementation of policy. It compares the myriad of subnational institutions. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 542 if student has credit for POLI 442.
POLI 542.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 500.d: This course introduces students to the practice of social science research including empirical description, theoretical development, and hypothesis generation and testing. It includes projects on the design and implementation of surveys, controlled experiments, archival data collection, fieldwork, case studies, and qualitative analysis.
POLI 500.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 562.d: This course offers a broad overview of urban politics and policies in cities around the world. We will examine how national, regional and local forces shape the processes and outcomes governance within and across cities and metropolitan areas, paying particular attention to critical problems and politics that affect urban centers: growth, immigration, class conflict, public order, service management, education, housing transportation, environmental protection, sustainability, land-use planning and spatial competition. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 562 if student has credit for POLI 464.
POLI 562.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 356.d: The course seeks to understand the relationship between political institutions and the representation of social interests in the policy-making process across a variety of national contexts. The course focuses on the politics behind policy choices and how policy-makers are held accountable in democratic contexts. Case studies will draw upon examples in the United States, Latin America, Europe and Asia.
POLI 356.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 433.d: The course aims to understand current challenges related to the US Congress -- such as party polarization and gridlock -- using the experience of the policy-making processes of other nations. In addition to recent discourse on failures of representation in Congress, the course covers politics in Europe, Latin America and Asia.
POLI 433.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 250.d: An interdisciplinary course exploring lives and well-being in the context of gendered international and domestic politics and economic processes. Emphasis on the implications of power relations at levels from the household to the global for women and men around the world (with particular attention to Asia). Cross-list: ASIA 251, SWGS 250.
POLI 250.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 333.d: This course will examine legislatures and parliaments in countries around the world, exploring their similarities and differences as well as the causes and consequences of these similarities and differences.
POLI 333.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 315.d: Exploration of U.S. voting behavior and elections. Includes consideration of both individual level behavior and aggregate level patterns of election results.
POLI 315.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 419.d: The goal of this seminar is to provide the student with knowledge of the formation, organization, activity, and impact of political parties and interest groups in the United States. Special attention will be given to changes in the operation of these two types of organizations over the last 20 years.
POLI 419.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 506.d: This course provides an analytic and quantitative framework to design and implement causal analysis, especially in observational studies. It focuses on understanding the logic, mathematical foundations and implications of causal reasoning using diverse frameworks, and covers tools for its implementation such as randomization, weighting, difference-in-difference, matching, and others.
POLI 506.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 354.d: Study of the political process in contemporary Latin America, with emphasis on selected major countries.
POLI 354.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 395.d: This course uses a lecture/lab combination to introduce students to research design, applied research methods, and statistical software in political science. Students will learn key skills and tools to conduct research in political science and have an opportunity to apply those in an individual or group project.
POLI 395.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 471.d: This course introduces students to key concepts, themes, and approaches in the study of protests, political violence, and government response from a global perspective. It surveys recent findings on the nexus of protest and repression. It also includes a research component, requiring students to pursue a research project on the topic.
POLI 471.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 310.d: This course is an interdisciplinary survey of the role that human biology plays in our political behavior. The biology covered ranges from genes to neural structures to neuro-chemistry, while the political behavior covered ranges from levels of participation to political beliefs to left/right ideology.
POLI 310.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 323.d: This course explores how the Supreme Court has interpreted and applied the US Constitution in the area of civil rights and liberties. We will examine claims related to property, privacy and personhood, First Amendment speech and religious protections, and equal protection of the laws based on race, gender, age, etc.
POLI 323.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 566.d: Graduate seminar that examines the theoretical and empirical literature on party development, organization, and change.
POLI 566.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 211.d: This course introduces students to major topics in the subfield of International Relations, including the causes of war, political dimensions of the international economy, international organizations, and interstate cooperation to address contemporary global challenges. This course helps students navigate upper division courses in International Relations and explore the international world.
POLI 211.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 350.d: This course examines the dynamics of urban politics and policy in an emerging global city - Houston. The lab is project-based and allows students to engage in hands-on, policy-focused research under the guidance of the faculty instructor. Weekly sessions will include lectures, case studies, guest lecturers, site visits, and work on research projects. POLI 350 requires either POLI 332 as a pre-requisite, which can be taken concurrently. POLI 337 may serve as a Co-Requisite for this course. Department Permission Required.
POLI 350.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 520.d: Core graduate course analyzing basic approaches to the study of comparative government.
POLI 520.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 535.d: Graduate seminar that examines the role of race and ethnicity in American politics. This course provides an examination of the behavioral and electoral implications of racial and ethnic diversity.
POLI 535.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 462.d: Seminar examining the process and substance of public policy across nations, with emphasis on social policy in industrialized democracies.
POLI 462.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 512.d: This seminar develops tools for the design and conduct of experiments in the social sciences. At the conclusion of the course each student will have developed and implemented an experiment testing some aspect of human social behavior.
POLI 512.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 381.d: The course examines Texas government, politics and society from the formation of the Texas Republic to the present. In addition to historical overviews, students will consult primary sources and utilize data from the Texas Legislative History Project to better understand key events, trends and dynamics in the Lone Star State.
POLI 381.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 305.d: Independent reading under the supervision of a full-time member of the department. Instructor Permission Required.
POLI 305.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 574.d: Introduction to a growing body of literature on how and why individual preferences dominate those of others. Includes the relationship between decision-making structures and the nature of decisional outcomes.
POLI 574.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 210.d: This course introduces students to major topics in the subfield of American Politics, including public opinion, group politics, political parties, elections, congressional-presidential-bureaucratic politics, and judicial politics. This course helps students navigate upper division courses in American Politics and understand American government and politics.
POLI 210.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 598.d: Individualized study on a specific topic in the field of Comparative Politics for Ph.D. students. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 598.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 456.d: This course will examine how formal and informal institutions and development processes have shaped gender inequality across the economic, social and political sphere. It will focus on theories and evidence from low and middle income countries.

POLI 343.d: Examines the role of media in politics. Attention is given to the media as a quasi-political institution. It elaborates the role the media plays in elections and the policy process.
POLI 343.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 338.d: Familiarizes students with the analytical tools necessary for evaluating and analyzing public policies. Cross-list: SOSC 301. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 338 if student has credit for POST 338.
POLI 338.pre: (SOSC 302 or STAT 310 or STAT 315 or ECON 209) and SOPA 309
POLI 338.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 348.d: The lab course examines urban politics and policy by combining urban theory and methods with an intensive focus on one or more case studies. In addition to social, political and economic issues, the course focuses on history, culture, language, and architecture. The lab features a field research trip to one or more cities (e.g, Istanbul), typically during spring break. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 348.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 337.d: Exploration of the role that public bureaucracy plays in national policy making. Includes an examination of sources of agency power, which are linked to different policy outcomes.
POLI 337.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 540.d: Core graduate course. Includes an analysis of basic approaches to the study of international relations.
POLI 540.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 316.d: This course examines key themes in American political thought and their implications for today, including the contested meaning of the Declaration of Independence, the controversy over ratification of the Constitution, and different approaches to confronting injustice, with a particular emphasis on slavery and its legacy.
POLI 316.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 371.d: This course seeks to examine the origins and dynamics of civil war, including civil war onset, duration, outcome, termination, why people join rebellions, the effectiveness of various forms of civil war management and resolution, and more. It aims to impart to students a solid understanding of theories and empirical evidence regarding the causes, conduct, and termination of civil wars in general.
POLI 371.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 473.d: This course will introduce students to the problems faced by intelligence analysts. Students will study historical examples of intelligence analysis. Placed in teams, they will monitor streams of actual events and provide assessments of these events.
POLI 473.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 600.d: Research and thesis for resident students. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 600.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 461.d: A research seminar focusing on women as political leaders worldwide. Topics include: leadership as a gendered concept; conditions that promote women’s inclusion in/exclusion from leadership posts; whether, when, and why women leaders behave differently than men; and citizens’ reactions to men and women in leadership roles.
POLI 461.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 421.d: This seminar will focus on major issues (e.g., immigration, voting rights, budget deficits, healthcare) in American society. After examining the history of national and state policies, seminar participant swill discuss social science contributions to the ongoing policy discussions. Specific topics covered will vary by semester.
POLI 421.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 476.d: In this research seminar, students explore key concepts and debates in political science such as power, authority, democratization, globalism, national security, and representation, as they emerge in a specific part of the world. The course includes a faculty-led site visit to another country in which students conduct their research first hand. Students learn how to conduct research in an international setting. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 476.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 317.d: Examines the role of Congress in the American political system. Attention is given to the historical development of Congress, the current status of the Congress, and the functions of Congress in the American political system.
POLI 317.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 362.d: This course offers a broad overview of urban politics and policies in cities around the world. We will examine how national, regional and local forces shape the processes and outcomes governance within and across cities and metropolitan areas, paying particular attention to critical problems and policies that affect urban centers: growth, immigration, class conflict, public order, service management, education, housing transportation, environmental protection, sustainability, land-use planning and spatial competition.
POLI 362.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 332.d: Exploration of issues of political behavior and public policy in urban and metropolitan areas. Includes urban decline, regional governance, revitalization, and issues of ethnic and racial conflict.
POLI 332.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 111.d: This course provides credit for students who have successfully completed approved examinations, such as the International Baccalaureate exam for Global Politics. This credit counts toward the total credit hours required for graduation only. This course is for transfer credit only.
POLI 111.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 475.d: Research seminar on theories and evidence of international cooperation. The course will explore conditions conducive to establishing and maintaining cooperation in international politics, the design of international agreements and institutions, and the influence of international agreements and institutions on international relations.
POLI 475.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 301.d: This course comparatively examines state governments and political institutions in the U.S. states. We will also focus on how state political institutions and organizations influence the creation, adoption, and implementation of public policy.
POLI 301.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 405.d: This is the first course in the Political Science Honors Program. Students will conduct independent research and prepare a formal research proposal for their planned thesis by the end of the semester. Students must complete both POLI 405 and 406 to get Honors in Political Science. Instructor Permission Required.
POLI 405.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 580.d: Topics vary from year to year. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 580.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 365.d: An examination of British politics and government, with emphasis on both the contemporary and historical setting. This course also emphasizes a comparison of the British political system with the American political system.
POLI 365.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 319.d: This course introduces students to the study of judicial systems around the world. In doing so, we will examine the role of courts in the modern state to better understand their growing importance as political actors. We will engage with different theories to compare how law, politics and judiciaries interact.
POLI 319.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 306.d: Independent reading under the supervision of a full-time member of the department. Instructor Permission Required.
POLI 306.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 529.d: This graduate seminar is designed as an overview of the major areas of inquiry in Urban Politics. The course will familiarize students with the principal questions and the methodological and theoretical approaches employed by scholars in this subfield. Recommended Prerequisite(s): POLI 502 and POLI 504
POLI 529.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 505.d: Special topics in political methodology. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 505.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 352.d: Mexico entered the 21st Century as one of the most dynamic societies in Latin America. But Mexico's fast-paced and chaotic transformation cannot be understood without a look at its past and its diverse cultural makeup. This course explores the weight of Mexico's history and culture as it seeks to forge ahead economically, socially, and politically.
POLI 352.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 378.d: The primary focus on this course is the use of military force in pursuit of the national security of the US. A wide variety of topics are covered including the people in the military, weapons of mass destruction, and various types of conflict that have involved (or might involve) the United States.
POLI 378.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 537.d: Study of the administration and implementation of public policies across federal, state, and substate governments.
POLI 537.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 430.d: Research seminar in the history of Texas politics.
POLI 430.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 431.d: Examines the role of campaigns in determining the outcome of political races.
POLI 431.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 565.d: This course looks at various theories of collective action and social movements. It will examine theoretical debates about why individuals and groups occasionally redress their grievances through protest and more often endure hardships passively. It will evaluate the relative merit of these theories in explaining cases of protest and passivity worldwide.
POLI 565.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 530.d: Core graduate course. Includes an analysis of basic approaches to the study of American politics.
POLI 530.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 432.d: Research seminar on political behavior and public policy in urban and metropolitan areas.
POLI 432.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 528.d: The course examines the theoretical and empirical study of institutions in political science. Its specific focus is on the study of American politics, with attention to the Congress, presidency, courts, and the media as institutions.
POLI 528.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 472.d: The content of American foreign policy, its sources, and the process of policy formulation.
POLI 472.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 468.d: This course explores the spatial nature of politics. It examines how policies, ideas and behaviors spread globally among political actors. Topics covered include: government and parties’ policy diffusion. The contagion of civil war and terrorism, the spread of protests and social movements, and the dynamics of economic globalization.
POLI 468.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 342.d: Explores the role of courts and judges in American politics. Will illustrate major characteristics of judicial institutions in the U.S. and provide understanding of forces influencing judicial decisions. Will cover federal and state organization of trial and appellate courts, judicial selection methods, and the politics of judicial decision-making.
POLI 342.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 564.d: A central priority developing nations face today concerns establishing economic growth; how best to achieve strong economic performance has both an economic and political dimension. This course seeks a rudimentary understanding of economic growth, concentrating on its political determinants.
POLI 564.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 355.d: Provides an introduction to politics in the Middle East. Brief historical overview is combined with detailed description of political systems in the area. The region is then used to examine empirically, critique, and revise theories of comparative politics. Emphasis on whether the region would be considered unique or exceptional.
POLI 355.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 576.d: Seminar surveying some of the primary theoretical perspectives and analytical approaches for studying international political economy. Includes a survey of contemporary literature, with special emphasis on theory and research, as well as instructions in how to critically evaluate research and set up a research project.
POLI 576.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 415.d: This course focuses on American political institutions. We will use current and historical research in political science to examine the inner-workings of Congress, the presidency, the judiciary, and inter-branch relations. Students can expect to gain insight into topics such as how scholars study elections, ideology, and oversight.
POLI 415.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 364.d: Focuses on three questions: (1) How do governments and other actors coordinate to regulate the cross-border flow of goods, services, and capital? (2) How do the resulting gains and losses drive political struggle? (3) Why is global exchange prone to crisis, and how do actors seek to manage volatility?
POLI 364.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 513.d: The major objectives of this course are to introduce graduate students to the skills and resources needed to design and conduct a survey.
POLI 513.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 575.d: Examination of current developments in game theory with application to political science.
POLI 575.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 594.d: Individualized study on a specific topic in the field of American Politics for Ph.D. students. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 594.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 102.d: This lab companion course to SOSC 302: Quantitative Analysis for the Social Sciences involves political science-specific applications of statistical analysis. The lab focuses on the use of software to analyze data from research in political science. Students who enroll in this lab section must also enroll in SOSC 302 during the same semester.
POLI 102.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 260.d: Advocating for change is an experiential learning course that teaches students how to engage in issue advocacy as a method of social change. Students work in teams with faculty mentors to develop and implement an advocacy plan for a particular cause or policy of interest. Cross-list: LEAD 260.
POLI 260.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 209.d: This course will examine constitutionalism and authoritarianism, including Plato, Machiavelli, and Marx, and introduce students to classical and contemporary political theories.
POLI 209.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 349.d: This course examines the dynamics of urban politics and policy in an emerging global city - Istanbul. In addition to social, political and economic issues, we will also focus on history, culture, language, architecture and the arts. Weekly class sessions will include lectures, case studies, guest lecturers, and group work on research projects. The lab also features an 8-day field research trip to Istanbul. Prerequisites may be taken the same semester as POLI 349/ASIA 349. Instructor Permission Required. Cross-list: ASIA 349.
POLI 349.pre: POLI 355 (may be taken concurrently) or POLI 362 (may be taken concurrently) or POLI 464 (may be taken concurrently) or POLI 562 (may be taken concurrently)
POLI 349.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 322.d: The aim of this course is to acquaint students with the major influences upon who gets what, when and how from American government. Major issues (e.g., health care, immigration, agriculture) covered will vary by semester. One component of the course will be devoted to assessing the impact of money on elections and the policy process.
POLI 322.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 324.d: Taught in English. Novels, and films, from North and West Africa, and the immigrant population in France, from 1960 to 2010. Emphasis on the tensions between narratives of political emancipation, modernity, secularism, and religious fundamentalism and mysticism. Extra reading for graduate students in theories of colonialism, postcolonialism, globalization. Cross-list: FREN 324, RELI 476. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for POLI 324 if student has credit for RELI 604.
POLI 324.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 440.d: This course provides students an opportunity to conduct original research on wide range of public policy questions. Students will be provided specific research questions to investigate over the course of the semester for which they will design and complete an original program of research.
POLI 440.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 372.d: Examination of internal and external aspects of foreign policy leadership, presidential initiative, congressional control, press, public opinion, and crisis management. Not a Managerial Studies elective.
POLI 372.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 438.d: Study of minority group politics and how race structures contemporary U.S. politics. Includes myths and realities of minority groups, symbolic politics and race, pluralism as a model of U.S. democracy, the intersection of class, race, and gender, civil rights movements, group consciousness, public opinion regarding minorities, and responses of national institutions to race issues.
POLI 438.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 328.d: Latinos and public policies affecting Latinos have become a major part of the discourse taking place in American politics as a result of current and projected demographic trends. After reviewing the demographic, historic, and social factors distinctive to the Latino population in the United States, this course examines how Latinos have interacted with political institutions to shape politics and public policy.
POLI 328.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 504.d: Study of applications of maximum likelihood estimation.
POLI 504.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 441.d: Common Property Resources (CPRs), such as fisheries, aquifers, and the Internet, appear in many guises and pose a fundamental problem for governing. Exploration of theoretical underpinnings for CPRs, their growing literature, and the political and economic institutions mediating CPR dilemmas. Included is an original research project in conjunction with the instructor. Cross-list: ENST 441.
POLI 441.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 569.d: In this course, we explore the conceptual meanings of democracy and representation, and then examine the theoretical and empirical linkages between citizen preferences, electoral systems, executive and legislative institutions, policymaking and advance industrial democracies. The aim of the course is to understand how citizen preferences ultimately get translated into policy outcomes and how political institutions shape this relationship.
POLI 569.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 581.d: Topics vary from year to year. Instructor Permission Required. Repeatable for Credit.
POLI 581.restr: Enrollment is limited to Graduate level students.

POLI 351.d: This course will venture to explore the “rich and diverse particularity” of Muslim political life at a time when Islam has become virtually synonymous with violence and hostility toward modernity. The topics include Islamic principles of government, relationship between political and religious authority, Islamism, Islam and democracy, jihad, and shariah.
POLI 351.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

POLI 112.d: This course provides credit for students who have successfully completed approved examinations, such as Advanced Placement exams. This credit counts toward the total credit hours required for graduation.
POLI 112.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.
